opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in layers, honestly. The first thing I'd say is that responsibility doesn't disappear just because something is open source. When you release weights, you are making a decision that has consequences, and you should own that decision. But the *shape* of the responsibility is different from a closed API provider's.

With a closed model, you sit in the middle of every request. You can filter, rate-limit, and ban accounts. With open weights, once the model is out, it's out. So most of your leverage comes *before* release. That means doing serious evaluations: red-teaming, testing for things like bio or cyber uplift, and understanding what the model can actually do that wasn't easily available before. If a model gives meaningful new capability for causing serious harm, that's a real reason to pause or change what you release. I don't think "open" should mean "release everything no matter what."

The second layer is what you ship alongside the weights. That includes a safety-tuned version, clear documentation of known limitations, acceptable use policies, and tools like classifiers or guard models that people building products can plug in. You can't force everyone to use them, but you can make the responsible path the easy default. In practice most developers *want* to do the right thing; they just need good building blocks.

The third layer, and I think people sometimes underestimate this, is that responsibility is shared across the ecosystem. The model provider is one party. The application builder who deploys it to millions of users has a lot of responsibility too, because they control the context, the user interface, and the monitoring. Cloud platforms, hosting services, and regulators all have a role. Trying to put 100% of the burden on the weight provider is a bit like asking the people who make compilers to prevent all malware. Some, yes, but not all of it.

And then there's the counterweight, which is the benefit of openness itself. Open models let researchers, including safety researchers, actually inspect and study these systems. They let smaller companies and other countries participate instead of depending on a handful of providers. Many problems get found and fixed faster because many eyes are on them. So when we talk about misuse, we should weigh the marginal risk of releasing a model against the marginal benefit. That should be done honestly, not ideologically in either direction.

So my short answer: an open-source provider is responsible for careful evaluation before release, for shipping good safety tooling and guidance, and for being transparent about risks. Downstream, the people who build and deploy products carry a big share of the responsibility, and the whole ecosystem has to mature together.

r001.rationale: It says released weights cannot be controlled afterward and that providers cannot force downstream developers to use safety tools, describing the limits of their practical control.

r002.rationale: It mentions regulators as part of the ecosystem, but does not assign policing harmful AI use to courts or law-enforcement agencies.

r003.rationale: It compares provider responsibility to compiler makers and malware, but does not make the kitchen-knife seller comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this in layers, because "responsibility" gets thrown around as if it's one thing, and it really isn't.

The first layer is the thing you can actually control at the source. When you train and release a model, you make choices about the data, the fine-tuning, the safety tuning, the red-teaming before release. Meta does a lot of that with Llama, and I think that's genuinely the right place to put effort, because it's the one point where the provider has full leverage. Once the weights are out, you don't get that leverage back.

The second layer is the license and the terms. An acceptable use policy is not nothing. It sets the norm, it gives you a basis to act against clear bad actors, and it tells the ecosystem what the provider considers out of bounds. But let's be honest, a license doesn't stop someone who's determined to misuse a model. It's a legal and social instrument, not a technical one.

And that brings me to the honest part, which is that with open weights, the provider's direct control essentially ends at release. You can't revoke a download. So I think the responsibility shifts, and it becomes a shared responsibility across the whole stack. The people who host it, the people who fine-tune it, the people who build applications on top of it, they all have a piece. My view from the infrastructure side is that a lot of the practical safety actually lives at the application and deployment layer. That's where you know the use case, the users, the context. A general model can't know if it's being used for customer support or something it shouldn't be.

I'd also push back a bit on the framing that open source is uniquely dangerous here. Closed models get jailbroken. Closed models leak. And the capability frontier is mostly set by the big labs, not by the open models, which usually trail by some months. What open source does is let a much wider community inspect the model, find the failure modes, and build the guardrails and tooling. I'd argue that on net, that transparency has been a safety benefit, not a cost.

So if you ask me what a responsible open-source provider owes the world, I'd say: do the hard safety work before release, be transparent about what the model can and can't do, set clear terms, stay engaged with the community after release, and be thoughtful about the actual risk level of what you're putting out. At the extreme frontier, I think it's fair to be more careful. But for the vast majority of models, the openness itself is part of how we keep the ecosystem healthy.

r001.rationale: It says that after open weights are released, the provider cannot revoke downloads or regain direct control, and that practical safety shifts to hosts, fine-tuners, and application builders.

r002.rationale: It describes shared responsibility across the ecosystem but does not assign harmful-use policing to courts or law-enforcement agencies.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison to a kitchen-knife seller or buyers’ use of knives.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a shared responsibility here. If you release an open-source model, you should evaluate potential misuse, explain the limitations, and give developers tools to build safeguards. You can’t simply say, “It’s open source, so whatever happens afterward has nothing to do with me.”

At the same time, the model provider can’t control every downstream application. The developer deploying it has responsibilities too, because they know the context: who is using it, what data it can access, and what actions it can take. A chatbot answering general questions and a system making consequential decisions need different protections.

Open source also lets more people inspect the technology, identify problems, and improve defenses. So I wouldn’t frame openness and safety as opposites. The question is how to make responsible development easier across that whole chain, while being honest that no safeguard can eliminate every possible misuse.

r001.rationale: The response says a provider “can’t control every downstream application,” clearly conveying practical limits on controlling downstream use.

r002.rationale: The response does not assign policing harmful AI use to courts or law-enforcement agencies.

r003.rationale: The response makes no comparison to a kitchen-knife seller or buyers’ use of knives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the responsibility is shared, but shared responsibility doesn’t mean that the model provider has no responsibility. If you release a model, you should evaluate its risks, explain its limitations, and provide safeguards and guidance that help people deploy it responsibly.

At the same time, an open-source model provider cannot control every downstream application. The developer building a product has more context about who is using it and what actions it can take. So there need to be protections at that level as well—access controls, monitoring, and restrictions appropriate to the application.

Open source also allows more people to inspect the model, identify problems, and improve the defenses. But transparency alone doesn’t prevent misuse. I would look at this as an ongoing responsibility across the whole ecosystem, rather than something you solve once when you release the model.

r001.rationale: It says an open-source provider “cannot control every downstream application,” conveying practical limits on enforcing downstream restrictions.

r002.rationale: It discusses shared responsibility and deployment safeguards but does not assign policing harmful use to courts or law-enforcement agencies.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison to a kitchen-knife seller or buyers’ use of knives.
